jen: Hey — running a replay harness against the new kernel-selection change and seeing ~15–20% worse p99 vs our synthetic client at the same nominal QPS. Anyone seen this pattern before? Here's the harness cmd we used: 

```
./replay-harness --trace session_XYZ --qps 80 --concurrency 40 --duration 600
```

It should be reproducing production arrival patterns. Perf-bot: profile attached (heap + cpu).

ben: hmm, first suspect is client-side connection behaviour. Are you reusing keepalive connections or creating a fresh TCP/TLS per request? small TLS handshakes will kill p99.

jen: we're replaying recorded client streams — the harness can either replay original connection boundaries or collapse them into a pooled client. For this run I left original boundaries intact to be "faithful". Maybe that backfired.

sam: that matters a lot. Synthetic clients often use a small pool (or HTTP/2/gRPC multiplexing) which hides TLS+TCP costs. Replay that preserves many short-lived connections will increase CPU (handshake) and TCP slow-start effects. Try enabling connection pooling in the harness: `--pool-mode pooled` and compare.

carla: also check KV-cache locality. Replay of long conversations tends to have much higher KV cache hit rates (shorter effective compute per token). If your synthetic traffic is mostly independent prompts, batcher/kernel selection will see different seq-len distributions and pick different kernels. That can change tail latency.

jen: good point. I looked at perf-bot flamegraph and saw lots of time in `ssl_handshake` and `epoll_wait`. But there's also a wider spread in batch sizes between the two runs. Synthetic run had steadier batch sizes around 8; replay had spikes (1, then 12).

ben: those spikes will trigger different kernel paths. Our runtime chooses kernels based on batch and seq len heuristics; uneven arrival patterns can force slower kernels or miss vectorization windows. For apples-to-apples you need to align: same arrival distribution, same connection reuse pattern, same prompt length distribution, and warmed KV caches.

sam: small extra gotcha: Nagle + TLS interactions. If client sends many tiny writes, enabling TCP_NODELAY on the client helps. HTTP/1.1 + small chunked bodies + Nagle can add ms-level delays that stack at p99. gRPC (http2) tends to pack streams better.

carla: and TLS resumption. If your replay creates new TLS sessions each time, check whether session tickets/resumption are enabled. With many short sessions, resumption cuts the handshake cost dramatically.

jen: actionable list so we don't re-run blind: 
- reproduce: run replay with `--pool-mode pooled` (reuse connections) and `--tls-resume enabled`.
- match token distribution: feed the same prompt-length histogram into synthetic generator.
- warm KV cache: pre-warm by replaying first N conversations before measuring.
- record batching stats: collect batch-size histogram from the runtime (route `/debug/batcher/stats`).
- tcp-level capture: `sudo tcpdump -w replay.pcap port 443` for a token of TLS handshakes.

ben: also try forcing `TCP_NODELAY` in the client for a run, and run the synthetic client with `--burstiness=match-replay` (Poisson vs uniform matters).

perf-bot: FYI there's a recent regression linked to kernel-selection heuristics on non-uniform batch sizes — internal ticket PERF-4579. Might be related.

sam: I'll run three variants tomorrow: 1) replay-original-conns (baseline), 2) replay-pooled-conns + tls-resume, 3) synthetic tuned to replay histograms + tcp_nodelay. Will attach batcher stats and pcap.

jen: perfect — I'll also dump KV hit-rate traces and share the model version + quantization profile. If p99 still differs, we can pin kernel selector to previous revision and see if that narrows the gap.

carla: quick snippet for comparing distributions (local):
```python
# approximate hist compare
from collections import Counter
print(Counter(replay.token_lengths).most_common(10))
print(Counter(synthetic.token_lengths).most_common(10))
```

jen: thanks all. One more note: when reporting apples-to-apples to the perf team, include connection churn metrics (new TLS sessions/min), average batch size, KV hit-rate %, and the exact client binary + flags. Those are the usual gotchas reviewers ask for. :thumbsup:

ben: and paste the raw harness command and env (LD_PRELOAD, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS) — threading at the client or system level can also skew results.

sam: ok assigning myself, will post results in this thread.

jen: awesome — assigning follow-ups to sam and jen. Thanks!
